title: How To Improve Classroom Management By Doing Less
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that teachers struggling with classroom management instinctively do more—talking, moving, raising their voice, micromanaging—when doing less would actually gain them more control. He offers six practices: slow down rather than rush through lessons, move less by staying in one place so students focus on the teacher, talk less and make words count, pause often to let students process directions, do nothing and simply wait in silence when the class isn't giving the expected response, and lower rather than raise the voice, since a raised voice trains students to only listen when a teacher is yelling. He also urges teachers to trust their classroom management plan to do the disciplinary work rather than resorting to pleading, persuading, or intimidating students. Linsin frames the whole approach as an example of working smarter rather than harder in classroom management.
points: Counterintuitively, doing less—slowing down, moving less, talking less—yields more classroom control than doing more.
Stay in one place rather than constantly moving around the room so students' attention stays focused on the teacher.
Pause often when giving directions, allowing students time to process information and giving the teacher a chance to check comprehension.
When students aren't responding as expected, do nothing: stand in a prominent spot and wait silently rather than escalating.
Lower your voice instead of raising it; a raised voice trains students to tune out until the teacher yells.
quotes: If you slow down, move less, talk less, and at times do absolutely nothing, you will gain more control. And classroom management won’t be such a challenge.
It’s always smart to take your time. If you rush or get ahead of your students, you’ll lose them—and control of your class.
The reality is, the more you talk, the less your students will tune in and the more likely they are to misbehave.
If your students aren’t giving you what you want, stop whatever you’re doing. Stand in the most prominent place in the classroom (I like to stand on a chair) and do nothing.
When you raise your voice, you train your students to listen to you only when you get loud and to tune you out the other times.
More than any other area of teaching, effective classroom management requires you to work smarter, not harder.
